sections.h2: Who handles what on a McDonald County tax bill
sections.html:
A McDonald County tax bill passes through two desks in the Pineville courthouse. The Assessor puts a value on property and answers appeals. The Collector mails the bills, receives the money and runs the sale of delinquent parcels.

  • Collector: 408 Harmon Street, Pineville, MO 64856. Letters: PO Box 725 (payments by mail can go here too). Phone (417) 223-7408.
  • Assessor: McDonald County Courthouse, 408 Harmon Street, Pineville. Letters: PO Box 726. Phone (417) 223-4361 for real estate and mapping.
  • Weekday hours are 8:00 am until 4:00 pm for both, with no break at noon. State holidays are days off.

Only the Assessor can change where a bill is mailed. Selling soon while statements still go to a former address? Fix that before the listing goes up.

The county occupies Missouri's southwest corner next to Arkansas and Oklahoma, and Pineville is the seat. About 23,992 people lived here in July 2025, 3.0 percent more than in 2020. The 9,940 housing units are mostly owned by their occupants (67.3 percent). A typical owned home is valued at $154,700, rent runs a median $767 and household income is $52,375. The McDonald County R-I School District covers most parcels while small areas belong to other districts, so read the district line on a bill when comparing homes.

State statute fixes January 1 as the date taxable parcels are valued, and the Missouri State Tax Commission oversees county assessors. What gets taxed is a fraction of market value, and the fraction varies with the class of property.

McDonald County assessment rates by property class
Property classAssessment rate
Residential19%
Agricultural12%
Commercial32%

A residential parcel is assessed at 19 percent, so the class on your record matters; a wrong class means a wrong bill, and the Assessor can review it. Each taxing body over the parcel then adds its own levy: schools, roads, cities, fire districts and a junior college among them. County government itself receives no property tax levy for operations and runs on sales tax.

RSMo 137.115 sets the reassessment cycle: new values take effect January 1 in odd-numbered years and stay through the following even year, except for new construction. An assessor must also inspect a residential parcel in person before raising it more than 15 percent, again leaving out new construction.

Personal property and real estate statements are mailed during the first week of November. You can pay the moment one arrives, and it turns delinquent once December 31 passes. This year's bills are already out, so the cutoff is December 31, 2026.

  • One check can cover every statement. Splitting a bill into pieces is not allowed.
  • Cash, a personal check, a money order or a card works, whether you pay in person, mail it or go online.
  • Mail postmarked after December 31 is sent back unless the late fees are enclosed.
  • If nothing has come by the end of November, call the Collector. A lost or missing bill still leaves the debt, penalty and interest in place.

Missouri adds a penalty to unpaid taxes after the delinquency date (RSMo 139.100). Before paying late, ask the Collector at (417) 223-7408 what penalty and interest percentages apply. Mailed payments count on the postmark date.

Each August the Collector holds the delinquent sale. A parcel with old unpaid years can head toward auction long before an owner notices.

sections.h2: How do I contest my McDonald County value?
sections.html:
Start by phoning the Assessor, (417) 223-4361, to request an informal review. Gather recent nearby sales, contractor repair quotes or photos that support a lower number, and write down the date and name of each person you speak with so you can follow up. Also ask when the local equalization board accepts filings.

If the board leaves your value alone, RSMo 138.430 lets you take the case to the State Tax Commission. The filing is due on the statutory date or 30 days after the board's final action, whichever comes later. Once an appeal is filed, the contested taxes are held in a separate fund instead of reaching the taxing bodies.

A second route is paying under protest. RSMo 139.031: settle the full bill before delinquency and hand the collector a written explanation of your objection. A protest becomes void if you file no circuit court suit against the collector within ninety days. An appeal already pending at the State Tax Commission stands in for that suit.

State revenue officials administer the Property Tax Credit Claim, nicknamed the circuit breaker. Some seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled get back part of what they paid in property tax or rent. The ceiling is $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters, and the exact credit depends on tax paid and household income of every kind. Questions can go to PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov.

One more break is a homestead exemption for a former prisoner of war who has a total service-connected disability. The home must be the owner's primary residence. Show the assessor the federal disability letter and discharge papers, or a records center letter that confirms the prisoner of war history.

Military personnel living here on orders, with a home of record elsewhere, generally owe no Missouri personal property tax on non-business items.

Treat the tax bill as a closing line item. Before you list, ask the Collector for the status of each year on the parcel. The closing agent will divide the current year between you and the buyer. Delinquent years can put a parcel in the August sale, so pay old balances first.

  • Check the name and address the Assessor has on record.
  • Request a payoff amount for each parcel in the sale, land and any manufactured home included.
  • Keep the settlement statement, since it shows how that year's tax was divided.
  • A value that seems too high should be raised with the Assessor before the board deadline, not once the sale is done.

Plan the order of calls this way. First phone the Collector for balances. Next ask the Assessor whether the name, address and class on the parcel are right. Then give both figures to the closing agent so the settlement statement matches. If a bill arrives after closing, the statement you saved shows who owed which share, and the Collector can confirm what was paid under the parcel.

Back taxes can stall a financed sale, because the title company wants an open balance resolved first. A cash buyer has no lender waiting on a clean tax record, so closing can move faster. The unpaid amount is still taken out of your proceeds at the table, and the Collector's payoff figure tells you how much.

faqs.q: What date makes a McDonald County tax bill late?
faqs.a: Anything unpaid after December 31. Bills go out the first week of November, and a payment postmarked in January comes back unless late fees are included.

faqs.q: Can I pay half of my bill now and half later?
faqs.a: No. The Collector cannot accept partial payment, though all statements can be paid together with a single check.

faqs.q: What assessment rate applies to a McDonald County house?
faqs.a: Residential property is assessed at 19 percent of market value. Farmland is 12 percent and commercial parcels are 32 percent, before any taxing body applies its levy.

faqs.q: Where do I send an address correction for my tax statement?
faqs.a: Call the Assessor at (417) 223-4361. The Collector's site routes address changes to that office.

faqs.q: When is the delinquent tax sale?
faqs.a: It happens each August at the Collector's office. For the exact date and the parcels offered, call (417) 223-7408.
